title: Senior's toolkit: surviving vim anywhere
summary: Saving, quitting, aborting a git message, root-owned files, swap files and CRLF scripts: the vim commands that get you out of trouble.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: surviving vim anywhere
steps.body: vim (or plain vi) is on every server and inside every container image that has an editor at all. These are the commands that get you in, out and unstuck.

toolkit.what: Back to normal mode, then save and quit. `:x` and `ZZ` only write when something changed, so the file's timestamp stays put otherwise.
flags: always safe: back to normal mode (Ctrl+[ does the same)
write only if changed, then quit

toolkit.what: Leave without saving, or throw away your edits and reload the file from disk.
flags: reload from disk, stay in the file
toolkit.when: you made a mess and want the original back

toolkit.what: Quit with an error exit code. git treats that as "cancel": `git commit` aborts and `git rebase -i` stops without changing anything.
toolkit.when: git opened vim and you want to back out of the commit or rebase

toolkit.what: Save a root-owned file you opened without sudo (`E45: 'readonly' option is set` or `E212: Can't open file for writing`). Works in vim; neovim cannot prompt for the password this way, so use `sudoedit` there.
flags: writes stdin to the file as root
hides tee's copy of the file on screen
toolkit.when: next time, open it with `sudoedit` instead

toolkit.what: Recover edits from a swap file after a crash or a dropped SSH session. The `E325: ATTENTION` screen offers the same: (R)ecover, then delete the old `.swp` once you have saved.
flags: on the E325 screen, when the swap is stale and nothing is lost

toolkit.what: Converts Windows line endings to Unix. A script saved with CRLF fails with `/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter`; this fixes it on the next `:w`.
flags: show the current file format (`dos` or `unix`)
toolkit.when: a script copied from Windows will not run

toolkit.what: Start vim without any vimrc or plugins. Tells you in seconds whether odd behaviour comes from your config.
flags: the same for vim and neovim

steps.prompt: Match each command to the situation it solves.
pairs: back out of a git commit message without committing
throw away edits and reload the file
save only if changed, then quit
get edits back after the SSH session died

steps.prompt: `./deploy.sh` fails with `/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory`. The script looks fine in vim. What do you do?
options: Open it in vim, `:set ff=unix`, then `:w`
steps.explain: The `^M` is a carriage return: the file has CRLF endings, so the kernel looks for an interpreter called `bash\r`. vim shows `[dos]` in the status line. In the repo, add `*.sh text eol=lf` to `.gitattributes` so it does not come back.

steps.prompt: You started `git rebase -i HEAD~5`, vim opened the todo list, and you realise you picked the wrong base. How do you leave so that nothing is rebased?
options: Delete every line, then `:wq`, and run `git reset --hard`
steps.explain: `:cq` exits with an error and git aborts the rebase before it starts. `:wq` would run the plan. (Deleting every line and saving also aborts, but `reset --hard` afterwards would throw away uncommitted work.)

steps.prompt: You edited `/etc/hosts` without sudo and vim refuses to write. Save it anyway.
steps.explain: `:w !cmd` pipes the buffer to a shell command. `%` is the current file name, and `sudo tee` writes it as root.

steps.prompt: vim shows `E325: ATTENTION` because your SSH session dropped mid-edit. Recover the edits safely.
lines: Press R to recover from the swap file
Quit, reopen the file and choose (D)elete it to remove the old swap file

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When in doubt press Esc, then `:q!` or `:cq`: you can always start again. For root files use `sudoedit` instead of `sudo vim`, and when a shell script will not run, check `:set ff?` before you look anywhere else.
